# ECG Means — full content index

> Your ECG report, explained in plain English. Reviewed by Dr. Faisal Irshad, MBBS (PMDC 54440-S).

## ECG Report Phrases

### Abnormal ECG: What It Means on Your Report
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/abnormal-ecg/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
"Abnormal ECG" is a summary line printed by the ECG machine's software. It means at least one measurement — rate, rhythm, an interval or a wave shape — fell outside the program's normal limits. It is not a diagnosis. Many abnormal readings turn out to be harmless variants once a clinician looks at the tracing and at you.

### Anterior Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/anterior-infarct-age-undetermined/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
"Anterior infarct, age undetermined" means the software saw Q waves or missing R waves in the chest leads over the front of the heart (V2–V4), a pattern that a past heart attack can leave. It cannot say when, or be certain it happened at all. Lead placement, thick heart muscle and bundle branch block commonly mimic it.

### Anteroseptal Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/anteroseptal-infarct/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
"Anteroseptal infarct, age undetermined" means the software saw a pattern across the front and middle of the chest leads (V1–V4) that a past heart attack can leave — combining the septal (V1–V2) and anterior (V3–V4) territories. It cannot date it or be certain it happened. Chest-lead placement, body build and bundle branch block are common innocent mimics.

### Biatrial Enlargement on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/biatrial-enlargement/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Biatrial enlargement means your ECG shows signs that both the right and left atria, the two upper chambers of the heart, are enlarged or under strain at the same time. It is not a disease in itself. It is a clue that both sides of the heart may be working harder, usually because of an underlying condition. It warrants a proper assessment, but it is not an emergency on its own.

### Borderline ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/borderline-ecg/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A "borderline ECG" means the machine found something just outside its normal limits, but not far enough to call the tracing abnormal. It is the software's way of saying "probably fine, worth a human glance". In people without symptoms it is most often a normal variant or a technical artefact.

### Brugada Pattern on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/brugada-syndrome/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Brugada syndrome is an inherited condition of the heart's sodium channels. It produces a characteristic pattern in the right chest leads of an ECG and carries a risk of dangerous heart rhythms. Many people with a Brugada pattern feel completely well. Even so, it always needs proper assessment by a heart specialist, especially if you have had fainting or a family history of sudden death.

### Early Repolarization on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/early-repolarization/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Early repolarization is a common normal variant in which the point where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins (the J point) sits slightly above the baseline, often with a small notch. It is seen in roughly 1 in 10 to 1 in 20 people, especially young adults, athletes and men, and in the great majority it is harmless.

### Hyperkalaemia on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/hyperkalemia-ecg/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Hyperkalaemia means a high level of potassium in your blood. An ECG cannot measure potassium directly, but certain patterns strongly suggest it and can show up before blood results are back. The key point is that hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated as a medical emergency, so the blood level is checked urgently and treatment does not wait.

### Hypokalaemia on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/hypokalemia-ecg/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Hypokalaemia means a low level of potassium in your blood. It leaves characteristic fingerprints on the ECG, mainly affecting the T wave, the U wave and the QT interval. It is usually very treatable, but it should be checked by a clinician. Low potassium can make the heart prone to abnormal rhythms, and ECG changes suggest the heart is already being affected.

### Inferior Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/inferior-infarct-age-undetermined/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
"Inferior infarct, age undetermined" means the software saw Q waves in the leads that look at the bottom (inferior) wall of the heart — II, III and aVF — a pattern a past heart attack can leave. It cannot say when, or be sure it happened at all. Small inferior Q waves are common in healthy people, so this is one of the more frequently over-called findings.

### Lateral Infarct: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/lateral-infarct/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
A "lateral infarct" on an ECG report means the software saw a pattern — usually Q waves — in the leads that look at the side wall of the heart (I, aVL, V5 and V6), which a past heart attack can leave. As with the other "age undetermined" infarct labels, it is a suggestion that needs a clinician's review and often an echocardiogram, because lead factors and normal variants can mimic it.

### Left Axis Deviation: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-axis-deviation/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Left axis deviation means the average direction of electrical flow through your ventricles points further up and to the left than usual — between −30° and −90°, where normal is −30° to +90°. It is a measurement rather than a disease, and as an isolated finding it usually needs no action.

### Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH): What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-ventricular-hypertrophy/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) means the main pumping chamber's muscle is thicker than normal. The ECG only measures the electricity, so it infers LVH from tall QRS complexes using "voltage criteria". These criteria miss many thick hearts and flag many normal ones — especially slim, young or athletic people — so the ECG statement is a prompt for an echocardiogram, not a diagnosis.

### Low Voltage QRS: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/low-voltage-qrs/
"Low voltage QRS" means the main spikes of your ECG are unusually small: under 5 mm in all six limb leads, or under 10 mm in all six chest leads. Either the heart is generating less signal, or — more commonly — something between the heart and the skin electrodes, such as fat, air or fluid, is dampening it.

### Nonspecific ST Abnormality on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/nonspecific-st-abnormality/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
"Nonspecific ST abnormality" means the ECG software noticed small changes in the ST segment or T wave that don't fit any specific diagnosis. It is one of the most common and least alarming phrases on a computer-read ECG. In someone who feels well and has no risk factors, it is usually benign. It matters more if it is new compared with an older ECG, or if you have symptoms such as chest pain or breathlessness.

### Nonspecific T Wave Abnormality: What It Means and Whether to Worry
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/nonspecific-t-wave-abnormality/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Few ECG phrases generate as many anxious searches as this one, and few are as frequently harmless. "Nonspecific" is the key word: the machine is telling you the T waves look slightly off, and also telling you that the way they look off does not match any known disease. The T wave is the part of the ECG most easily nudged by everyday things — a cold drink, a fast breath, a skipped meal, a worrying thought. This page explains what the report is describing, whether it is serious, every cause worth knowing, what "inferior" means if that word appears, and what your doctor will actually do.

### P Mitrale on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/p-mitrale/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
"P mitrale" on your ECG report means the P wave looks broad and notched, like a letter "M". This pattern suggests the left atrium, the upper-left chamber of the heart, may be enlarged. It is a marker of a strained or enlarged left atrium rather than a disease in itself. It is not an emergency, but it is worth checking with a heart scan.

### P Pulmonale on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/p-pulmonale/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
'P pulmonale' on an ECG report describes a tall, peaked P wave that suggests the right upper chamber of the heart (the right atrium) may be enlarged. The name comes from its classic link with lung ('pulmonary') disease that strains the right side of the heart. It is a clue rather than a diagnosis, and it is not an emergency on its own. It is worth having a clinician look into the cause.

### Pericarditis on an ECG: What It Shows
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/pericarditis-ecg/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Pericarditis is inflammation of the sac around the heart. On the ECG it classically produces widespread, saucer-shaped (concave) ST elevation across many leads, together with PR-segment depression. The key task for a clinician is to separate it from a heart attack, which also raises the ST segment but in a different pattern. The ECG is only part of the picture, alongside symptoms and blood tests.

### Poor R Wave Progression: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/poor-r-wave-progression/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
"Poor R wave progression" means the upward R wave does not get taller as it should from chest lead V1 to V4 — typically the R wave in V3 is 3 mm or less. It can be a trace left by an old heart attack on the front of the heart, but far more often it reflects electrode position, body build or a normal variant.

### Possible Left Atrial Enlargement: ECG Meaning
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-atrial-enlargement/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
"Possible left atrial enlargement" means the P wave — the small bump before each QRS — is wider or more notched than usual, a shape that can occur when the left upper chamber of the heart is stretched or under pressure. The ECG is a poor judge of chamber size, so this is a hint, not a measurement; an echocardiogram gives the real answer.

### Possible Right Atrial Enlargement: ECG Meaning
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-atrial-enlargement/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
"Possible right atrial enlargement" means the first part of your P wave — the bit made by the right upper chamber — is taller and more peaked than usual, a pattern called P pulmonale. Like its left-sided counterpart it is only a hint from the P wave shape; the ECG judges chamber size poorly, so an echocardiogram gives the real answer.

### Posterior MI: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/posterior-mi/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
A posterior MI is a heart attack affecting the back wall of the heart. Standard ECG leads do not look directly at this area, so it shows up as mirror-image changes — ST depression and tall R waves in the front chest leads (V1–V3). It is easy to miss, which is why it is important, and it needs urgent treatment like any heart attack.

### Pulmonary Embolism on an ECG: What It Shows
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/pulmonary-embolism-ecg/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
A pulmonary embolism (PE) is a blood clot in the lungs. The ECG can show clues — most often a fast heart rate, sometimes the classic S1Q3T3 pattern or signs of right heart strain — but no single ECG finding confirms or excludes a PE. A normal ECG does not rule it out, so suspected PE always needs proper testing.

### Right Axis Deviation: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-axis-deviation/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Right axis deviation means the average direction of electrical flow through your ventricles points further to the right than usual — beyond +90°, where normal is −30° to +90°. It can be a normal variant in tall, slim young people, but it is also a classic sign of strain on the right side of the heart, so it is read together with the rest of the tracing.

### Right Heart Strain: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-heart-strain/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Right heart strain (right ventricular strain) means the right side of the heart is working hard against raised pressure in the lungs. On the ECG it shows as T-wave inversion in the right chest leads (V1–V3) and other right-sided changes. It is a clue to look for an underlying lung or pulmonary-artery problem, most urgently a pulmonary embolism.

### Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH): What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-ventricular-hypertrophy/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) means the smaller, right-sided pumping chamber has thickened, usually because it is working against high pressure in the lungs. On the ECG the normally small right ventricle starts to dominate, giving a tall R wave in lead V1 and a rightward axis. The ECG is insensitive to it, so an echocardiogram is the test that confirms it.

### Septal Infarct on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/septal-infarct/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
"Septal infarct" means the ECG software saw a pattern in chest leads V1–V2 that can be left behind by a past heart attack affecting the septum, the wall between the ventricles. It is one of the most frequently over-called findings. Misplaced chest electrodes and normal variation produce the same pattern in people who have never had a heart attack.

### Sgarbossa Criteria: Finding a Heart Attack in LBBB
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sgarbossa-criteria/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
The Sgarbossa criteria are three ECG signs that help doctors spot a heart attack (STEMI) when the usual signs are hidden by a left bundle branch block (LBBB) or a pacemaker. A normal LBBB already distorts the ST segments, so these rules look for changes that go beyond what the block alone would cause. If your report mentions them, it is in the context of a possible heart attack and needs urgent care.

### Wellens Syndrome: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/wellens-syndrome/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
Wellens syndrome is a specific pattern of T-wave changes in the chest leads (V2–V3) that warns of a critically narrowed left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. It often appears when chest pain has settled, which can be falsely reassuring. It is a red-flag pattern that needs urgent cardiology assessment because a large heart attack may be close.

## Heart Rhythms

### Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm (AIVR) on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/accelerated-idioventricular-rhythm/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) means your heartbeat was being set by a pacemaker site in the ventricles, the heart's lower chambers, instead of its usual starting point. It runs faster than the heart's normal backup (escape) rhythm but slower than ventricular tachycardia. It is classically seen as a benign 'reperfusion rhythm' after a blocked coronary artery reopens. It is usually harmless in itself, but the underlying cause, such as a heart attack, still needs proper care.

### Accelerated Junctional Rhythm: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/accelerated-junctional-rhythm/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Accelerated junctional rhythm is a rhythm arising from the AV junction at 60–100 beats per minute — faster than the junction's natural 40–60, so it outpaces the sinus node. The QRS is narrow and normal-looking but the P waves are missing or upside-down. It usually signals irritation of the junction by a drug, recent surgery or reduced blood supply.

### AFib with RVR: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/afib-with-rvr/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
AFib with RVR means atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response — the heart is in atrial fibrillation and the ventricles are being driven unusually fast, usually over 100 beats per minute. On the ECG it looks irregularly irregular, with no clear P waves and closely spaced, normal-shaped QRS complexes. It is common and treatable, but a fast rate needs assessment.

### Ashman Phenomenon: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ashman-phenomenon/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Ashman phenomenon is a single wide beat that happens when a short cycle follows a longer one, causing one beat to be conducted abnormally (aberrantly) through the bundle branches. It is most often seen in atrial fibrillation and is harmless in itself — its importance is that it can be mistaken for a premature ventricular beat.

### Atrial Bigeminy: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-bigeminy/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Atrial bigeminy means the ECG shows a repeating pattern where every normal beat is followed by a premature atrial contraction (PAC) — an early beat from the upper chambers. It is very common, usually harmless, and often felt as skipped beats. A doctor may still check for triggers if it happens a lot.

### Atrial Fibrillation: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-fibrillation/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Atrial fibrillation (AF or AFib) is the most common sustained abnormal heart rhythm. The upper chambers quiver instead of beating in an organised way, so the pulse becomes irregular and often fast. On the ECG there are no normal P waves and the QRS complexes are irregularly spaced. It is rarely immediately life-threatening, but it raises the risk of stroke and needs proper assessment.

### Atrial Flutter: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-flutter/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Atrial flutter is a fast, usually regular rhythm in which the upper chambers beat in a rapid, organised circle — around 300 times a minute — while the AV node lets only a fraction through to the ventricles. On the ECG it produces a distinctive "sawtooth" baseline. It is a close relative of atrial fibrillation and carries a similar stroke risk.

### Atrial Tachycardia: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-tachycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Atrial tachycardia is a fast heart rhythm — usually 150–250 beats per minute — driven by a single focus in the atria rather than the normal sinus node. On the ECG each QRS is preceded by an abnormally shaped P wave. It is a form of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) and, while rarely immediately dangerous, it should be assessed because a persistently fast rate can tire the heart.

### AV Dissociation: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/av-dissociation/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
AV dissociation means the atria and the ventricles are beating independently of each other, each driven by its own pacemaker, rather than in the normal coordinated way. It is a description rather than a single diagnosis — it can be benign or a sign of a serious conduction problem — so the cause needs to be identified.

### Bigeminy: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/bigeminy/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Bigeminy means every second heartbeat is a premature (extra) beat, so beats arrive in pairs: normal, early, pause; normal, early, pause. Usually the extra beats are PVCs from the lower chambers — ventricular bigeminy. It can feel like a slow or thumping pulse. In a structurally normal heart it is generally benign.

### Ectopic Atrial Rhythm: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ectopic-atrial-rhythm/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
An ectopic atrial rhythm means the heartbeat is being started by a site in the atria other than the sinus node. The rhythm is regular and the QRS normal, but the P waves look different from usual — sometimes small, flat or inverted. At a normal rate it is often a harmless variant; it takes on more importance only when it is fast or persistent.

### Ectopic Beats on an ECG: What They Mean
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ectopic-heartbeat/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
An ectopic beat is an extra heartbeat that starts somewhere other than the sinus node, the heart's usual starting point. 'Ectopic' simply means 'out of place.' Ectopic beats are extremely common, and most healthy people have some. Occasional ectopic beats are harmless and do not shorten life, even though they can feel alarming.

### Fusion Beat: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/fusion-beat/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A fusion beat happens when the heart is activated from two directions at once — the normal pathway from above and a ventricular beat from below meet in the middle, producing a single hybrid-shaped beat. Fusion beats are usually harmless in themselves, and they are a helpful clue that confirms a ventricular rhythm.

### Idioventricular Rhythm: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/idioventricular-rhythm/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
An idioventricular rhythm is a slow rhythm, usually 20–40 beats per minute, generated by the ventricles themselves when no impulse reaches them from above. The QRS complexes are wide and there are no related P waves. The accelerated form (AIVR), at roughly 50–110 per minute, is commonly seen for a short time after a blocked coronary artery is reopened and is usually harmless.

### Junctional Bradycardia: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-bradycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Junctional bradycardia means a slow heart rhythm that is being driven from the AV junction (the area around the AV node) rather than the normal sinus pacemaker, usually at a rate below about 40 beats per minute. It can be a normal back-up rhythm or a sign that the sinus node or AV conduction is not working well, so the context matters.

### Junctional Escape Rhythm on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-escape-rhythm/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
A junctional escape rhythm is a backup rhythm that starts in the AV junction, around the AV node, when the heart's usual pacemaker (the sinus node) fails to pace the heart or its impulses are blocked. It is a safety mechanism, not a primary problem in itself, and on its own it often causes no symptoms. What matters most is finding out why the sinus node stopped leading.

### Junctional Rhythm: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-rhythm/
A junctional rhythm means the heartbeat is being started by the AV junction — the relay point between the upper and lower chambers — instead of the usual sinus node. It typically runs at 40–60 beats per minute with a normal narrow QRS but no normal P wave in front. It is a back-up rhythm that appears when the sinus node slows or is blocked.

### Junctional Tachycardia: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-tachycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Junctional tachycardia is a fast rhythm — over 100 beats per minute — that arises from the AV junction, the relay point between the upper and lower chambers, instead of the sinus node. The QRS is narrow but the P waves are missing or inverted. It is the fast end of the junctional-rhythm family and usually signals an irritated junction from a drug, surgery or illness.

### Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia (MAT): What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/multifocal-atrial-tachycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is a fast, irregular rhythm in which several different sites in the atria fire in competition, producing at least three distinct P wave shapes at a rate over 100. It is strongly associated with serious lung disease and other acute illness, so although the rhythm itself is rarely the main danger, it is a marker that the person is unwell.

### Paced Rhythm on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/paced-rhythm/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
A paced rhythm means an implanted pacemaker is generating some or all of your heartbeats. The report is describing the pacemaker's output, not a disease, so it tells you the device is doing its job. A normally functioning paced rhythm is expected and reassuring. Concern arises only if there are signs the device is not working properly or you develop new symptoms such as dizziness or fainting.

### Premature Junctional Contraction on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/premature-junctional-contraction/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A premature junctional contraction (PJC) is an early extra beat that starts in the AV junction rather than the sinus node, the heart's usual pacemaker. It is a less common relative of the premature atrial and ventricular beats, and it is usually a benign finding. Occasional PJCs are harmless and do not need treatment. Frequent ones are worth a closer look, because they can occasionally point to digoxin toxicity or heart strain.

### Premature Ventricular Contraction (PVC) on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/premature-ventricular-contractions/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A premature ventricular contraction (PVC) is an early extra beat that starts in the ventricles, the heart's lower pumping chambers, rather than in the sinus node, the heart's natural pacemaker. PVCs are one of the most common findings on any ECG and are usually benign, especially in a structurally normal heart. They deserve a closer look mainly when they are very frequent, come in runs, or happen alongside symptoms such as fainting or chest pain.

### R-on-T Phenomenon: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/r-on-t-phenomenon/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
R-on-T phenomenon means a premature ventricular beat (PVC) falls very early — right on top of the previous beat's T wave. The T wave marks a vulnerable moment in the heart's electrical cycle, so a beat landing there can occasionally trigger a dangerous fast rhythm. It is worth a careful review, especially when the heart is already stressed.

### Sick Sinus Syndrome on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sick-sinus-syndrome/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Sick sinus syndrome (also called sinus node dysfunction) means your heart's natural pacemaker, the sinus node, no longer reliably sets a normal rate. This can show up as a heart rate that stays too slow, pauses between beats, or fast rhythms that alternate with slow ones. It is not an emergency unless there is collapse, but it does need a clinician's review. It matters most when it causes symptoms such as dizziness or fainting.

### Sinus Bradycardia: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-bradycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Sinus bradycardia is a normal heart rhythm at a rate below 60 beats per minute. The beat starts in the right place and travels the normal route; it is simply slow. It is normal during sleep and in physically fit people, and is only a problem if the rate is too slow to meet your body's needs.

### Sinus Pause and Sinus Arrest: What They Mean
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-pause-arrest/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
A sinus pause (or sinus arrest) is a gap in which the heart's natural pacemaker, the sinus node, briefly fails to fire, so no beat is produced for a moment. Short pauses are common and usually harmless, especially during sleep or in athletes. Long pauses, or pauses that cause dizziness or fainting, point to sinus node disease and may need a pacemaker.

### Sinus Rhythm With PACs: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-rhythm-with-pac/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
"Sinus rhythm with PACs" means your underlying rhythm is normal, with occasional early beats arising from the upper chambers (premature atrial complexes, also called contractions). Almost everyone has some. They may be felt as a skipped beat or flutter and are harmless in the great majority of people.

### Sinus Rhythm With Sinus Arrhythmia: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-arrhythmia/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Sinus arrhythmia is a normal, harmless variation in which the heart speeds up slightly as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out. Despite the word "arrhythmia", it is not a rhythm disorder. It is most obvious in children, young adults and fit people, and indicates a healthy, responsive nervous system.

### Sinus Rhythm: What It Means on Your ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-rhythm/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Sinus rhythm is the normal rhythm of the heart. It means each heartbeat is being started by the heart's natural pacemaker, the sinus node, and travelling through the normal pathway. "Normal sinus rhythm" adds that the rate is between 60 and 100 beats per minute. The word "sinus" has nothing to do with your nose.

### Sinus Tachycardia: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-tachycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Sinus tachycardia is a normal heart rhythm at a rate above 100 beats per minute at rest. The heart's own pacemaker is simply firing faster, nearly always as a response to something — exertion, anxiety, pain, fever, dehydration, caffeine or illness. It is a sign to look for the trigger rather than a heart rhythm disease in itself.

### Supraventricular Tachycardia on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/supraventricular-tachycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is a fast heart rhythm that starts at or above the AV node, in the upper chambers or the junction, rather than in the lower chambers (the ventricles). It usually begins and ends suddenly. SVT can feel unpleasant, but it is rarely dangerous in an otherwise healthy heart, and recurrent episodes can very often be cured. Because it can sometimes need urgent treatment, a doctor should review it.

### Trigeminy: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/trigeminy/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Trigeminy is a repeating pattern in which every third heartbeat is a premature (extra) beat: normal, normal, early, pause. When the extra beats come from the lower chambers it is ventricular trigeminy, the usual form. It reflects frequent PVCs falling into a regular pattern and, in an otherwise healthy heart, is generally harmless.

### Ventricular Bigeminy: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-bigeminy/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Ventricular bigeminy means the ECG shows a repeating pattern where every normal beat is followed by a premature ventricular contraction (PVC) — an early, wide beat from the ventricles. It often feels like skipped beats or a flip-flop in the chest. It is frequently harmless, but a doctor should check how often it occurs and whether the heart is otherwise normal.

### Ventricular Couplet: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-couplet/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
A ventricular couplet means two premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) occur back-to-back — two early, wide beats from the ventricles in a row. Isolated couplets are common and often harmless in a normal heart, but frequent couplets, or couplets with heart disease, deserve a closer look because they sit a step closer to longer ventricular runs.

### Ventricular Fibrillation on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-fibrillation/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
Ventricular fibrillation (VF) means the lower chambers of the heart (the ventricles) are in a chaotic, disorganised electrical storm. The heart muscle quivers instead of pumping, so there is no effective heartbeat and no pulse. This is a cardiac arrest and is immediately life-threatening. VF is also one of the few truly reversible arrest rhythms if CPR and defibrillation are started within minutes.

### Ventricular Tachycardia on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-tachycardia/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a fast heart rhythm that starts in the ventricles, the heart's lower pumping chambers, instead of following the normal electrical pathway. Because the ventricles beat fast and inefficiently, VT can lower blood pressure and can turn into a more dangerous rhythm that causes cardiac arrest. It is a potentially life-threatening rhythm and doctors treat it as an emergency. With prompt assessment and treatment, it can be stabilised and its underlying cause addressed.

### Ventricular Trigeminy: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-trigeminy/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Ventricular trigeminy means the ECG shows a repeating pattern of two normal beats followed by a premature ventricular contraction (PVC) — an early, wide beat from the ventricles. Like bigeminy, it is often harmless, especially in a normal heart, but a doctor should check how frequent the PVCs are and whether the heart is otherwise healthy.

### Wandering Atrial Pacemaker: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/wandering-atrial-pacemaker/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A wandering atrial pacemaker means the spot that starts each heartbeat drifts between the sinus node and other sites in the atria, so the P waves change shape from beat to beat. The heart rate stays normal (under 100). It is usually a benign finding related to normal changes in vagal tone, and is common in the young, the old and athletes.

## Heart Blocks & Conduction

### 2:1 AV Block: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/2-1-av-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
In 2:1 AV block, exactly every other impulse from the upper chambers is blocked, so only one in two P waves is followed by a heartbeat — producing a pulse that is half the atrial rate. The catch is that a single strip cannot tell whether it is the benign (Mobitz I) or the more serious (Mobitz II) type, so 2:1 block is always assessed carefully.

### Bifascicular Block: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/bifascicular-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Bifascicular block means two of the three main conduction branches that carry the electrical signal to the ventricles are blocked. The usual combination is a right bundle branch block plus one of the two left-sided fascicles. On its own it often causes no symptoms, but it reflects disease in the heart's wiring and sometimes needs monitoring.

### Incomplete Left Bundle Branch Block: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/incomplete-left-bundle-branch-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Incomplete left bundle branch block means the left branch of the heart's electrical system is partly delayed — the QRS has an LBBB-like shape but is not yet fully widened. It is less well defined than a complete block and is often a marker of early conduction-system or left-heart changes rather than an acute problem.

### Incomplete Right Bundle Branch Block on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/incomplete-right-bundle-branch-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Incomplete right bundle branch block (IRBBB) means there is a mild, partial delay in the right bundle branch, the wiring that carries electrical signals to the right ventricle. It has the same shape as a full right bundle branch block, but the QRS is not quite wide enough to call it complete. In young, healthy people it is a very common and usually benign finding. In a well person with no symptoms, it usually needs no treatment.

### Intraventricular Conduction Delay (IVCD): What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/intraventricular-conduction-delay/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
An intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD) means the impulse takes longer than normal to spread through the ventricles, widening the QRS, but the pattern does not fit a typical left or right bundle branch block. When reports add the word "nonspecific," it simply means the delay has no classic shape. It is common, often mild, and its importance depends on the cause.

### Left Anterior Fascicular Block: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-anterior-fascicular-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Left anterior fascicular block (LAFB, or left anterior hemiblock) means one of the two small branches of the left bundle — the anterior fascicle — is delayed. The result is a marked leftward shift of the QRS axis with only slight widening of the QRS. It is a common finding, particularly with age, and on its own is generally harmless.

### Left Bundle Branch Block: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-bundle-branch-block/
Left bundle branch block (LBBB) means the electrical impulse cannot travel down the left branch of the heart's wiring, so the left ventricle is activated late and indirectly. On the ECG the QRS becomes wide (120 ms or more) with a characteristic shape. Unlike its right-sided counterpart, LBBB is usually associated with underlying heart disease and prompts an echocardiogram.

### Left Posterior Fascicular Block: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-posterior-fascicular-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Left posterior fascicular block (LPFB, or left posterior hemiblock) means the posterior branch of the left bundle is delayed. It is much less common than its anterior counterpart, and because the posterior fascicle is short, thick and well-supplied with blood, a block there usually means there is genuine underlying heart disease. It shifts the QRS axis to the right and is a diagnosis of exclusion.

### Lown-Ganong-Levine (LGL) Syndrome
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/lown-ganong-levine-syndrome/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Lown-Ganong-Levine (LGL) syndrome is an old term for a short PR interval on the ECG together with a normal, narrow QRS (no delta wave) and episodes of fast heartbeat. It is a form of suspected pre-excitation. The concept is debated today, but if your report mentions it, the key issue is the fast-heartbeat episodes, which deserve assessment.

### Right Bundle Branch Block: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-bundle-branch-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
Right bundle branch block (RBBB) means the impulse is delayed in the right branch of the heart's wiring, so the right ventricle is activated a little late. The QRS widens and takes on an "M-shaped" rSR' pattern in lead V1. Incomplete RBBB (QRS 110–119 ms) is a common normal variant, particularly in young people; complete RBBB is usually harmless too but is worth checking once.

### Second Degree AV Block Type 1 (Wenckebach): What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/second-degree-av-block-type-1/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Second degree AV block type 1 — also called Mobitz I or Wenckebach — is a pattern in which the delay through the AV node grows longer with each beat until one impulse fails to get through and a beat is dropped, after which the cycle restarts. The block is in the AV node itself, and in most people it is benign, especially when it appears during sleep or in athletes.

### Second Degree AV Block Type 2 (Mobitz II): What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/second-degree-av-block-type-2/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
Second degree AV block type 2 — Mobitz II — is a pattern in which some impulses from the atria are suddenly not conducted to the ventricles, with no warning lengthening of the PR interval beforehand. The block sits below the AV node in the bundle branches, which makes it unpredictable and liable to progress to complete heart block. It is one of the ECG findings that usually leads to a pacemaker.

### Sinoatrial (SA) Block on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinoatrial-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Sinoatrial (SA) block means your heart's natural pacemaker, the sinus node, fires normally, but its signal is delayed or blocked on its way to the upper chambers (the atria). The result is a missing or delayed heartbeat. Brief, occasional SA block, especially in young, fit people at rest or asleep, is usually harmless and causes no symptoms. It matters more if the pauses are long or frequent enough to make you dizzy, tired or faint.

### Sinus Rhythm With 1st Degree AV Block: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/first-degree-av-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
First degree AV block means every impulse from the upper chambers still reaches the lower chambers, but it takes slightly longer than normal to get through the AV node — a PR interval longer than 200 ms (one large square). Nothing is actually blocked. In most people it is a benign finding that needs no treatment.

### Third Degree (Complete) Heart Block: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/third-degree-av-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
Third degree AV block — complete heart block — means the electrical connection between the upper and lower chambers has failed completely. The atria and ventricles beat independently, and the heart relies on a slow back-up (escape) rhythm to keep going. It is the most serious of the AV blocks and usually needs urgent assessment and a pacemaker.

### Trifascicular Block: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/trifascicular-block/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Trifascicular block refers to disease affecting all three of the branches that carry the electrical signal to the ventricles. In practice the term is most often used for a bifascicular block (two branches) together with a delay in the third, shown as a long PR interval. It reflects widespread conduction-system disease and needs careful assessment.

### Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW): What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/wolff-parkinson-white/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) means there is an extra electrical connection (an accessory pathway) between the upper and lower chambers of the heart. On the ECG it shows as a short PR interval and a slurred start to the QRS called a delta wave. Many people never have symptoms, but WPW can cause fast heart-rhythm episodes, so it is always worth a cardiology review.

## Intervals & Waves

### Aberrant Conduction on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/aberrant-conduction/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Aberrant conduction (aberrancy) means a heartbeat that started normally in the upper part of the heart travelled through the lower chambers by an unusual route, so it looks wide on the ECG. It usually happens because one of the heart's wiring branches was still recovering when an early beat arrived. Aberrancy itself is benign. It is a normal electrical quirk, not heart damage. Its main importance is that it must be told apart from a genuinely ventricular beat or rhythm, because the two are managed very differently.

### Biphasic T Wave: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/biphasic-t-wave/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
A biphasic T wave is one that goes in two directions — partly up and partly down — instead of being a simple single hump. What it means depends on the order and the leads: an up-then-down T wave in the chest leads after chest pain can be an important warning sign (Wellens pattern), while a down-then-up T wave is more often linked with low potassium or a minor change.

### De Winter T Waves: What They Mean on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/de-winter-t-waves/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
De Winter T waves are a pattern of upsloping ST depression leading into tall, symmetrical T waves across the chest leads (V1–V6). They are considered a “STEMI-equivalent” — a sign of a blocked left anterior descending (LAD) artery — even though there is no classic ST elevation. The pattern needs the same urgent treatment as a heart attack.

### Delta Wave: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/delta-wave/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
A delta wave is a slurred, gradual upstroke at the very start of the QRS complex. It is the signature of an extra electrical connection between the upper and lower chambers (an accessory pathway) that lets the impulse bypass the normal AV node delay. Combined with a short PR interval, a delta wave is the Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pattern, which should be assessed by a cardiologist.

### Electrical Alternans: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/electrical-alternans/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Electrical alternans means the height of the QRS complexes changes from one beat to the next in a regular alternating pattern. Its best-known cause is a large collection of fluid around the heart (a pericardial effusion), in which the heart swings within the fluid so that each beat is recorded from a slightly different position. It can also occur with very fast rhythms. New electrical alternans deserves prompt assessment.

### Epsilon Wave: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/epsilon-wave/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
An epsilon wave is a small, low-amplitude deflection that appears just after the QRS complex, in the early part of the ST segment. It is best known as a marker of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), a condition that can cause dangerous rhythms, so it always warrants specialist assessment.

### Fragmented QRS: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/fragmented-qrs/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
A fragmented QRS means the QRS complex has extra notches or spikes rather than a smooth shape, reflecting scarred or diseased heart muscle that slows and splinters the electrical signal. It is often a subtle marker of previous heart damage and can carry prognostic information, so it is interpreted alongside your history and other tests.

### Hyperacute T Waves: What They Mean on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/hyperacute-t-waves/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
Hyperacute T waves are tall, broad, often symmetrical T waves that can be the very first ECG change of a heart attack — appearing even before the classic ST elevation. Because they can come and go quickly and precede obvious changes, they are an important early warning sign that needs urgent assessment when chest symptoms are present.

### Inverted P Wave on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/inverted-p-wave/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
An inverted P wave means the upper chambers of the heart (the atria) were activated in an abnormal direction, usually because the heartbeat started somewhere other than the sinus node, the heart's normal pacemaker. It is a clue to where a beat began, not a disease in itself. Often the explanation is benign, such as a junctional rhythm or limb leads that were simply swapped when the ECG was recorded.

### J-Point Elevation on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/j-point-elevation/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
"J-point elevation" means the point where the QRS complex ends and the ST segment begins sits slightly above the baseline on your ECG. In young, healthy people it is most often part of benign early repolarisation, a normal variant, rather than a sign of a heart attack. What matters is the overall pattern, whether it is new, and whether you have symptoms such as chest pain.

### Osborn Wave (J Wave): What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/osborn-wave/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
An Osborn wave — also called a J wave — is an extra positive deflection or notch at the junction where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins (the J point). Its classic cause is hypothermia (a dangerously low body temperature), and the colder the person, the larger the wave. It also appears with high blood calcium and some other conditions, and it typically disappears as the cause is corrected.

### Pathological Q Waves: What They Mean on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/pathological-q-waves/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
Pathological Q waves are abnormally deep or wide Q waves that usually indicate scar from a previous heart attack. Small, narrow Q waves can be completely normal, so the distinction matters. On their own, pathological Q waves often reflect an old, healed event rather than an emergency, but they should be interpreted by a doctor.

### Peaked T Waves: What They Mean on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/peaked-t-waves/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
Peaked T waves are T waves that are taller and more pointed than usual. They have two very different meanings: in a well person they are often a harmless normal variant (or early repolarization), but when they appear acutely they are the earliest ECG sign of a high blood potassium level (hyperkalaemia), which can be dangerous. The context decides which it is.

### PR Interval: Normal Range and What Short or Long Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/pr-interval/
Verdict/quick answer: A normal PR interval is 120–200 ms (0.12–0.20 seconds), or 3–5 small squares on standard ECG paper.
A normal PR interval is **120–200 ms** (0.12–0.20 seconds), or 3–5 small squares on standard ECG paper. It is the time from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS — how long the impulse takes to travel from the atria, through the AV node, to the ventricles. Longer than 200 ms is first degree AV block; shorter than 120 ms may mean an accessory pathway or a junctional origin.

### QRS Interval: Normal Range and What a Wide QRS Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/qrs-interval/
Verdict/quick answer: Normal is under 120 ms — less than three small squares — and many cardiologists prefer under 100–110 ms. A wide QRS means the impulse took a slow route: usually a bundle branch block, a beat starting in the ventricle, a pacemaker, or a drug or electrolyte effect.
The QRS interval (or duration) is how long it takes the electrical impulse to spread through both ventricles. Normal is under 120 ms — less than three small squares — and many cardiologists prefer under 100–110 ms. A wide QRS means the impulse took a slow route: usually a bundle branch block, a beat starting in the ventricle, a pacemaker, or a drug or electrolyte effect.

### QT and QTc Interval: Normal Range and Prolonged QT
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/qt-interval/
Verdict/quick answer: Normal QTc is under about 440 ms in men and 460 ms in women; over 500 ms is clearly prolonged and raises the risk of torsades de pointes.
The QT interval is the time the ventricles take to activate and then recover. Because it naturally shortens at faster heart rates, the machine corrects it for rate and prints the QTc. Normal QTc is under about 440 ms in men and 460 ms in women; over 500 ms is clearly prolonged and raises the risk of a dangerous rhythm called torsades de pointes.

### QT Prolongation on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/qt-prolongation/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
QT prolongation means the QT interval, the time your heart's lower chambers (the ventricles) take to contract and then reset electrically, is longer than normal. The number doctors actually judge is the rate-corrected value, called the QTc. A long QT doesn't usually cause symptoms by itself. It is a warning sign worth taking seriously because it can set the stage for a dangerous heart rhythm, and the cause can often be found and corrected.

### S1Q3T3: What the Pattern Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/s1q3t3/
Verdict/quick answer: Needs clinician review
S1Q3T3 describes a combination of three findings — an S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III, and an inverted T wave in lead III. It is best known as a textbook sign of a pulmonary embolism (a clot in the lungs), but it is neither sensitive nor specific: most people with a PE do not have it, and it can appear in healthy people. It is a prompt to think about PE in the right setting, not a diagnosis.

### Short PR Interval on an ECG: Causes, Meaning and When It Matters
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/short-pr-interval/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
"Short PR interval" is one of the more unsettling lines to find on an ECG report, partly because it sounds precise and partly because the internet links it to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. The reality is more reassuring: a short PR on its own, with a normal-looking QRS and no symptoms, is common and usually means nothing more than fast conduction through the AV node. This page explains what the measurement is, every cause worth knowing about, how to tell the harmless version from the one that needs attention, and what your doctor will do next.

### ST Depression: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/st-depression/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
ST depression means the ST segment — the flat part just after the QRS — sits below the baseline. Its most important cause is reduced blood flow to the heart muscle (ischaemia), but it also appears with a thick ventricle, digoxin, a fast heart rate and low potassium. The pattern of leads, whether it is new, and your symptoms decide how much it matters.

### ST Elevation: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/st-elevation/
Verdict/quick answer: Seek prompt care
ST elevation means the ST segment — the flat part just after the QRS — sits above the baseline. In the setting of chest pain it is the hallmark of a major heart attack (a STEMI) and is a time-critical emergency. But ST elevation also has several harmless causes, such as early repolarization and the normal pattern in some leads, so it is always read together with your symptoms.

### T Wave Inversion: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/t-wave-inversion/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
T wave inversion means the T wave points downward instead of upward. In some leads (aVR, V1, and often III) that is completely normal. In others it can be a normal variant, a sign of strain from a thick ventricle, a bundle branch block effect, or evidence of reduced blood supply or a recent heart attack. Which leads are involved, and whether it is new, decide its meaning.

### U Wave: What It Means on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/u-wave/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
A U wave is a small, rounded bump that sometimes follows the T wave on an ECG. Small U waves are a normal finding, most visible at slow heart rates and in the chest leads. Prominent U waves are the ones that matter — they are a classic sign of a low blood potassium level and of certain medicines.

### Wide QRS Complex on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/wide-qrs-complex/
Verdict/quick answer: Depends on context
A wide (broad) QRS complex means the heart's main pumping chambers, the ventricles, took longer than normal to activate electrically. It is a description, not a diagnosis, so what it means depends entirely on the cause. A long-standing bundle branch block in a well person can be harmless. A new wide QRS with chest pain, or a fast wide-complex rhythm, is treated urgently.

## Comparisons

### Atrial Fibrillation vs Atrial Flutter on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/afib-vs-aflutter/
Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter are two related fast rhythms that start in the heart's upper chambers (the atria). In atrial fibrillation the atria quiver chaotically, while in atrial flutter they beat in a fast, organised circle. Both carry the same kind of stroke risk and are assessed the same way for stroke prevention. Both are well-recognised and treatable, so the key next step is a conversation with your doctor about rhythm treatment and whether you need anticoagulation.

### EKG vs Echocardiogram: What's the Difference?
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ekg-vs-echocardiogram/
Verdict/quick answer: An EKG records the heart's electrical activity over about ten seconds using stickers on the skin; an echocardiogram is an ultrasound scan that shows the heart's structure and pumping.
An EKG (ECG) records the heart's electrical activity over about ten seconds using stickers on the skin; it shows rhythm, conduction and electrical signs of strain or damage. An echocardiogram is an ultrasound scan that shows the heart's structure and pumping — chamber sizes, wall thickness, valves and ejection fraction. They answer different questions, which is why an abnormal EKG is often followed by an echo.

The EKG is the electrical tracing; the echocardiogram is an ultrasound picture of the heart itself.

### Left vs Right Bundle Branch Block on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/lbbb-vs-rbbb/
Left and right bundle branch block both mean that one of the two main electrical cables to the heart's lower chambers (the ventricles) is blocked. That side of the heart is activated a little late, which makes the QRS complex on your ECG wider. The key difference is which cable is affected. Right bundle branch block is frequently benign, especially in a well person, while left bundle branch block more often points to underlying heart disease and is usually looked into further.

### PVC vs PAC: What's the Difference?
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/pvc-vs-pac/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A PAC (premature atrial contraction) is an early beat that starts in the upper chambers and travels the normal route, so its QRS looks normal. A PVC (premature ventricular contraction) starts in the lower chambers and spreads abnormally, giving a wide, odd-shaped QRS. Both are common and usually harmless; PVCs are the ones more often counted and followed up.

### STEMI vs NSTEMI on an ECG: What the Difference Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/stemi-vs-nstemi/
STEMI and NSTEMI are both types of heart attack (myocardial infarction), and the difference between them comes down to what the ECG shows. A STEMI usually means a coronary artery is completely blocked, while an NSTEMI usually means a severe but not complete blockage. Both are serious and both are emergencies. Telling them apart matters because it sets how quickly treatment needs to happen. If you have chest pain or pressure, breathlessness, sweating, or pain spreading to your arm or jaw right now, call emergency services immediately.

### SVT vs VTach: What's the Difference?
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/svt-vs-vtach/
Verdict/quick answer: SVT (supraventricular tachycardia) is a fast rhythm that starts above the ventricles and produces narrow QRS complexes; it is uncomfortable but rarely dangerous in a healthy heart. VTach (ventricular tachycardia) starts in the ventricles, produces wide QRS complexes, and is potentially life-threatening. Any wide-complex tachycardia is treated as VT until proven otherwise.
SVT (supraventricular tachycardia) is a fast rhythm that starts above the ventricles and produces narrow QRS complexes; it is uncomfortable but rarely dangerous in a healthy heart. VTach (ventricular tachycardia) starts in the ventricles, produces wide QRS complexes, and is potentially life-threatening. Any wide-complex tachycardia is treated as VT until proven otherwise.

## ECG Basics

### How to Read Your ECG Report: A Plain-English Guide
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/how-to-read-ecg-report/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
An ECG report has three parts: a block of measurements (rate, PR, QRS, QT/QTc, axis), a list of automated findings, and an overall verdict such as Normal, Borderline or Abnormal ECG. The measurements are reliable; the findings are over-sensitive suggestions; the verdict is only as good as the most significant finding. This guide walks through each part.

### If My ECG Is Normal, Is My Heart OK?
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/if-ecg-is-normal-is-my-heart-ok/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A normal ECG is reassuring: it makes an acute heart attack, a serious rhythm disturbance during the recording, and significant conduction disease unlikely. But it is a ten-second electrical snapshot. It cannot see blocked arteries that are not currently causing damage, mild valve disease, or a rhythm problem that comes and goes. Whether your heart is OK depends on what question is being asked.

### Wandering Baseline on an ECG: What It Means
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/wandering-baseline-ecg/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
A "wandering baseline" on your ECG report is an artifact, not a heart problem. It means the flat line the ECG traces drifted slowly up and down during the recording, usually because of breathing, movement or a poor electrode contact. It is harmless in itself. The only reason it matters is that heavy drift can hide or mimic real changes, which is why the ECG is often simply repeated.

### What Is an EKG (ECG)? A Plain-English Guide
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/what-is-an-ekg/
Verdict/quick answer: Usually harmless
An EKG — also written ECG — is a quick, painless test that records the electrical signals your heart makes with each beat. Small sticky pads on your chest, arms and legs pick up the signals, and the machine prints them as a set of waves. It takes only a few minutes, uses no needles and no radiation, and shows your heart's rhythm, rate and electrical health at that moment.

## ECG Tools & Calculators

### ECG Axis Calculator
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-axis-calculator/
Verdict/quick answer: The normal QRS axis is −30° to +90°. If the QRS is mainly upright in both lead I and aVF, the axis is normal. Upright in I but negative in aVF suggests left axis deviation unless lead II is also upright (0° to −30°, still normal); negative in I but upright in aVF suggests right axis deviation.
The QRS axis is the average direction of electrical flow through the ventricles. Enter the net size of the QRS in leads I and aVF (upward deflection minus downward deflection, in small boxes or mm), and the calculator estimates the axis in degrees.

### How to Calculate Heart Rate on an ECG
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-heart-rate-calculator/
Verdict/quick answer: For a regular rhythm, divide 300 by the number of large boxes between two R waves, or 1500 by the number of small boxes. For an irregular rhythm, count the R waves in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10. A resting rate of 60–100 bpm is normal.
Every ECG report prints a heart rate, but you can also work it out from the tracing itself. Choose a method below, enter what you count on the strip, and the calculator converts it to beats per minute.

### Normal ECG Values (Adults)
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/normal-ecg-values/
Verdict/quick answer: Normal adult ECG values: heart rate 60–100 bpm, PR interval 120–200 ms, QRS under 120 ms, QTc under about 440 ms (men) or 460 ms (women), and QRS axis −30° to +90°.
Every number printed at the top of an ECG report has a normal range. This chart puts them all in one place for adults, with links to what it means when a value falls outside it.

### QTc Calculator (Corrected QT Interval)
URL: https://www.ecgmeans.com/qtc-calculator/
Verdict/quick answer: QTc corrects the QT interval for heart rate. Bazett: QTc = QT ÷ √RR. Fridericia: QTc = QT ÷ ∛RR (RR in seconds). A QTc under about 440 ms in men and 460 ms in women is normal; over 500 ms is clearly prolonged.
Enter the QT interval and the heart rate (or RR interval) from your ECG report. The calculator gives the corrected QT (QTc) by the four standard formulas and shows where the result sits against the usual normal ranges.
